procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 17, 1964 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 597 of 1963, setting aside the acquittal of the appellant and directing his retrial.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A private party filed a revision application in the Patna High Court against the acquittal of the appellant by the Sessions Judge. The High Court, in its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, went into the evidence minutely, questioned the Sessions Judge's findings, and gave its own interpretation of the evidence de novo. The High Court then directed the retrial of the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order for retrial. The Supreme Court considered whether the High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, acted in accordance with the principles settled by the Supreme Court for interference with acquittal by way of revision filed by a private party.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can set aside an acquittal and order a retrial by re-appraising the evidence as if it were an appeal.

facts: The appellant was acquitted by a Sessions Judge.
A private party filed a revision petition in the High Court against this acquittal.
The High Court, exercising its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, set aside the acquittal and ordered a retrial.

In doing so, the High Court minutely re-examined and re-appraised the evidence, questioned the Sessions Judge's findings, and substituted its own interpretation, essentially treating the revision as an appeal.
law: The Supreme Court reiterated the established legal principles governing a High Court's revisional powers over an acquittal.
Interference is permissible only in exceptional cases, such as a "manifest illegality" in the judgment or a "gross miscarriage of justice."

Specific grounds for interference include glaring procedural defects, such as the trial court lacking jurisdiction, shutting out admissible evidence, considering inadmissible evidence, or completely overlooking evidence.

A High Court cannot set aside an acquittal in revision simply because it disagrees with the trial court's appreciation of the evidence or believes a wrong view of the law was taken. It is not a substitute for an appeal.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had not followed these settled principles.
The High Court did not identify any manifest illegality or gross procedural defect in the Sessions Judge's decision.
Instead, the High Court improperly acted as an appellate court by re-weighing the evidence from its own perspective and reaching different conclusions than the Sessions Judge.
The Court noted that the High Court's approach was incorrect, especially since the government had not chosen to appeal the acquittal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had exceeded its limited revisional jurisdiction by re-appraising the evidence as if it were an appeal. Therefore, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order for a retrial, and restored the original acquittal by the Sessions Judge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in exercising its revisional powers under s. 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, can set aside an acquittal and order a retrial by re-appraising the evidence as if it were an appeal.
appellant_arguments: The High Court erred by treating a revision application as if it were an appeal against acquittal, making no distinction between its appellate and revisional powers.
The High Court improperly went into the evidence minutely, questioned every finding of the Sessions Judge, and gave its own de novo interpretation of the evidence.
The Sessions Judge acted within his rights in acquitting the accused, as his decision was based on a proper appraisal of evidence that he found to be unsatisfactory and doubtful.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's intervention was justified because the Sessions Judge's acquittal was based on a flawed appraisal of the evidence.

The Sessions Judge committed an error of law by stating that defence witnesses should have been cross-examined with reference to their police statements, which warranted the High Court's interference.
The High Court correctly re-interpreted the evidence and found it acceptable, contrary to the opinion of the Sessions Judge, thus justifying the order for a retrial.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a revision filed by a private party against an acquittal, a High Court can only set aside the acquittal and order a retrial if there is a manifest illegality, a gross miscarriage of justice, or a glaring defect of procedure. A High Court is not entitled to interfere simply because it disagrees with the lower court's appreciation of evidence or its view on a point of law, nor can it re-weigh the evidence to reach a contrary conclusion.
obiter: By ordering a retrial, the dice is loaded against the accused because it is always difficult for the subordinate court to re-weigh the evidence while ignoring the opinion of the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In fact on reading the judgment of the Hi:;!; Court it is apparent to us that the learned Judge has re-weighed the evidence from his own point.of view and reached inferences contrary to those of the Sessions Judge on almost every point. This we do not conceive to be his duty in dealing in revision with an acquittal when Government has not chosen to file an appeal against it. In other words, the learned Judge in the High Court has not attended to the rules laid down by thi~ Court and has acted in breach of them.
legal_tests_applied: To set aside an acquittal in revision, there must exist a manifest illegality in the judgment of the Court of Session ordering the acquittal or there must be a gross miscarriage of justice.

The High Court is entitled in revision to set aside an acquittal if there is an error on a point of law or no appraisal of the evidence at all; it is not sufficient to say the judgment is 'perverse' or 'lacking in true correct perspective'.

Interference in revision with an order of acquittal can only take place if there is a glaring defect of procedure such as the court lacking jurisdiction, shutting out admissible evidence, considering inadmissible evidence, or overlooking some evidence.
why_respondent_won: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by treating the revision as an appeal, re-weighing the evidence from its own point of view, and reaching inferences contrary to those of the Sessions Judge on almost every point.

The High Court's interference did not meet the established legal standards, as there was no manifest illegality, gross miscarriage of justice, error on a point of law, or glaring procedural defect in the Sessions Judge's acquittal order.
The Sessions Judge acted within his rights in acquitting the accused based on a proper appraisal of evidence that he found to be unsatisfactory and doubtful.
policy_considerations: By ordering a retrial after expressing a strong opinion on the evidence, the dice is loaded against the accused, because it is always difficult for the subordinate court to re-weigh the evidence ignoring the opinion of the High Court.
